corruption_summary: The use of images in worship is itself the corruption—the Romish and Eastern veneration of statues, crucifixes, and icons, defended as honoring God through representations, which the second commandment forbids as idolatry.
corruption_paragraphs: The use of images in worship is itself the corruption that the second commandment forbids, and it has flourished in the Roman and Eastern churches in the form of statues, crucifixes, paintings, and icons venerated as aids and objects of devotion. Rome and the East defend the practice by distinguishing the veneration (dulia) offered to images and saints from the worship (latria) due to God alone, holding that the honor paid to the image passes to its prototype and that images serve as ‘books for the unlearned’ and windows to devotion. The Reformed reply on several grounds: that the commandment forbids the making and bowing to images in worship outright, without the subtle distinctions; that the distinctions, however carefully drawn by theologians, are not observed by the people, who do in fact worship the image; that God cannot be represented without dishonoring His infinite, invisible, spiritual nature; and that the golden calf, an image of the true God, was condemned as idolatry though Israel meant to worship the LORD by it.

The deeper principle is the spirituality of true worship and the sovereignty of God in appointing how He will be worshipped. God is a Spirit, infinite and invisible, and to reduce Him to a likeness of wood, stone, or paint is to distort and dishonor Him, exchanging the glory of the incorruptible God for an image. He has appointed the means of His worship—the Word, the sacraments, prayer, and praise—and the introduction of images as objects or aids of worship is both a violation of His command and a corruption of the spiritual worship He requires. The Reformers, applying the second commandment, stripped the images from their churches, not from any hatred of beauty or art (which have their lawful place), but from a jealous regard for the purity of worship and the honor of God, who has said, ‘I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.’ The recovery of the doctrine guards the church’s worship from idolatry and preserves the worship of the invisible God in spirit and in truth, by the means He has appointed, without images of any kind.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on the second commandment’s ban on the pesel (graven image) and tēmūnāh (likeness)—for God, a Spirit (pneuma), is worshipped without representation.

Israel’s golden calf was an image of the true God, yet condemned as idolatry—intention does not sanctify a forbidden practice.

etymology: “Reverence” from Latin reverentia, “awe, respect,” from revereri, “to stand in awe of,” from re- (intensive) + vereri (to fear, respect).
biblical_def: Reverence in worship is the godly fear, awe, and holy respect with which the creature must approach the worship of the holy God—a deep sense of His majesty, holiness, and greatness that produces humility, seriousness, and carefulness in drawing near to Him. Scripture everywhere requires it: ‘let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear: for our God is a consuming fire’; ‘God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him’; ‘the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him’; ‘worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth.’ Reverence flows from a right apprehension of who God is—the infinite, holy, majestic Lord before whom the seraphim veil their faces and cry ‘Holy, holy, holy,’ before whom Isaiah was undone, before whom Moses removed his shoes and the elders fall down. To approach such a God carelessly, flippantly, or irreverently is to dishonor Him and to forget what worship is. Reverence does not mean cold, joyless solemnity or mere external propriety; it is fully consistent with joy, even with exuberant praise—the saints rejoice before God with trembling, and worship Him with gladness—but it is joy mingled with awe, gladness that never forgets the greatness of the God who is its object. Reverence governs the manner of worship: the seriousness of approach, the carefulness to worship as God directs, the humility of the suppliant, the attentiveness of the hearer, and the holy gravity that befits the presence of the Most High. It must be guarded on two sides. Against irreverence—the casual, flippant, entertainment-driven, overly familiar approach that treats God as a buddy and worship as a show, forgetting His holiness and majesty. And against a dead, formal solemnity that has the outward forms of gravity without the inward fear and love of God. True reverence is the fruit of a heart that truly knows God—awed by His holiness, humbled by His majesty, and yet drawn near in glad love through Christ—and it ought to mark every approach to Him, that we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REVERENCE as fear mingled with respect and esteem; veneration; the holy awe and respect due to God, especially in worship.
webster_full: REVERENCE, n. — 1. Fear mingled with respect and esteem; veneration. ...Reverence is nearly equivalent to veneration, but expresses something less of the same emotion. It differs from awe, which is an emotion compounded of fear, dread or terror, with admiration of something great. We feel reverence for a parent, and for an upright magistrate, but we stand in awe of a tyrant. This distinction may not always be observed.
REVERENCE, v.t. — To regard with reverence; to regard with fear mingled with respect and affection; to venerate.

Psalm 89:7
God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him.
Habakkuk 2:20

Psalm 2:11

corruption_summary: Reverence is corrupted by the casual, flippant, entertainment-driven worship that treats God as a buddy and forgets His holiness—and, oppositely, by the cold, dead formalism that has the forms of solemnity without the inward fear and love of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Reverence in worship is corrupted, in our day most pervasively, by the casual and flippant familiarity that has overtaken much modern worship. God is addressed and spoken of as a buddy or a therapist; worship is styled as a relaxed, entertaining, comfortable experience; the gravity, awe, and holy fear that Scripture requires are dismissed as stuffy and off-putting; and the consuming fire before whom the seraphim veil their faces is approached with a breeziness that would be thought rude before an earthly dignitary. This forgets who God is—the infinite, holy Lord of heaven and earth—and what worship is—the creature’s awed approach to the Most High. Irreverence dishonors God, trivializes worship, and betrays a heart that has lost its vision of His majesty. The familiarity that breeds it is not the warm intimacy of the child with the Father (which is reverent love) but the careless contempt of the soul that no longer trembles.

Reverence is corrupted, on the other side, by a cold and dead formalism that wears the outward forms of solemnity—hushed tones, grave faces, stately ceremony—without the inward reality of the fear and love of God. This is reverence’s hollow imitation: the body bowed while the heart is far off, the appearance of awe without its substance, gravity that is mere decorum rather than the trembling of a soul that beholds its God. True reverence is neither the flippant familiarity of the casual nor the cold propriety of the formalist, but the godly fear of a heart that truly knows God—awed by His holiness, humbled by His majesty, yet drawn near in glad love through Christ. It is fully consistent with joy—indeed with exuberant praise—for the saints rejoice before God with trembling; but it is joy that never forgets His greatness. The recovery of reverence restores to worship its proper gravity and awe: we approach a consuming fire, and must serve Him acceptably with reverence and godly fear, our gladness mingled always with the holy trembling that befits the presence of the Most High.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on serving God with reverence (eulabeia, godly caution) and fear (deos)—the LORD greatly to be feared (Hebrew yārē’) in the assembly.

usage: Reverence in worship is the godly fear and awe with which the creature approaches the holy God—‘our God is a consuming fire.’

etymology: “Family” from Latin familia, “household”; “worship” from Old English weorþscipe. The daily worship of God in the household.
biblical_def: Family worship is the daily worship of God in the household—the gathering of the family, led by its head, for the reading of Scripture, prayer, praise, and instruction in the things of God. It occupies the middle place between public worship (the church assembled) and private worship (the individual alone), and it is a duty of great importance, deeply pressed in Scripture and central to the Reformed and Puritan tradition. God committed to the family the religious nurture of its members: Abraham was commended because he would ‘command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD’; the fathers were charged to teach God’s words diligently unto their children, talking of them when they sit in the house and when they walk by the way, when they lie down and when they rise up; and Joshua resolved, ‘as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.’ Family worship is the appointed means by which this charge is fulfilled day by day. Its elements are simple and biblical: the reading of a portion of Scripture, prayer (for the family, the church, the world), the singing of praise, and the instruction and catechizing of the children in sound doctrine. Its leadership belongs to the head of the household—the father, where there is one—who acts as the prophet, priest, and (under God) ruler of his little flock, leading them in worship and answering to God for their souls’ instruction. Its frequency is daily, morning and evening being the traditional pattern, that the household may begin and end its days with God. The blessings of faithful family worship are immense: the saturation of the home with the Word of God, the religious instruction of the rising generation, the binding of the family together in the things of God, the cultivation of piety in the young, and the calling down of God’s blessing upon the household. Its neglect—the abandonment of the family altar so widespread today—leaves the religious nurture of children to the church alone (a few hours a week) or to no one, and is a chief cause of the irreligion of the rising generation. The recovery of family worship is among the most urgent needs of the church and the home: that fathers would again lead their households daily before God, raising their children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
webster_summary: Webster 1828, under WORSHIP and FAMILY, notes family worship as the religious worship of God performed in a family or household, distinguished from public and private worship.
webster_full: FAMILY, n. — 1. The collective body of persons who live in one house and under one head or manager; a household, including parents, children and servants.
Family worship is the daily worship of God conducted in the household, consisting of reading the Scriptures, prayer, and praise, led by the head of the family.

And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house.
Genesis 18:19

Joshua 24:15

Ephesians 6:4

corruption_summary: No major postmodern redefinition, but family worship is widely abandoned—the family altar forsaken, the religious nurture of children outsourced to the church alone or neglected entirely, leaving fathers abdicating their God-given charge.
corruption_paragraphs: Family worship is corrupted in our day chiefly by sheer abandonment—the near-total collapse of the family altar that once stood at the center of Christian households. Where fathers formerly gathered their families daily, morning and evening, to read the Scriptures, pray, and praise God, the practice has largely vanished, even among professing believers. The causes are many: the busyness and fragmentation of modern family life, the loss of the father’s sense of his spiritual headship, the assumption that religious instruction is the church’s job rather than the home’s, and the simple neglect of a duty no longer pressed or modeled. The consequence is grievous: the religious nurture of children is left to a few hours of church a week, or to no one at all, and a generation grows up in Christian homes that are functionally godless from Monday to Saturday.

This abandonment is a chief cause of the irreligion of the rising generation and a great dishonor to God, who committed to the family the daily nurture of its members in His ways. The recovery of family worship is among the most urgent needs of the church. Scripture lays the charge plainly: fathers are to teach God’s words diligently to their children, to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, to command their households after them in the way of the LORD. The means is simple and within the reach of every household: a daily gathering for the reading of Scripture, prayer, praise, and the instruction of the children, led by the head of the family as the prophet, priest, and ruler of his little flock. The blessings are immense—the home saturated with the Word, the young instructed in sound doctrine, the family bound together in the things of God, and the divine blessing called down upon the household. The recovery of the doctrine summons fathers to take up again their abdicated charge, and to lead their families daily before God, that their children may be raised from the cradle in the fear and admonition of the Lord.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on the charge to teach diligently (shānan) God’s words to one’s children in the house, raising them in the nurture (paideia) of the Lord.
usage: Family worship is the daily worship of the household—Scripture, prayer, praise, and instruction—led by the head of the family.

The abandonment of the family altar leaves the religious nurture of children outsourced or neglected—a chief cause of generational irreligion.

etymology: “Private” from Latin privatus, “set apart, belonging to oneself”; “worship” from Old English weorþscipe. The individual believer’s personal worship of God.
biblical_def: Private worship is the personal, individual worship of God by the believer alone—the whole of his secret devotion, comprising private prayer, the reading and meditation of Scripture, praise, self-examination, and communion with God in the closet. It is the third sphere of worship, alongside public worship (the church assembled) and family worship (the household), and it is the most hidden and personal of the three. Its charter is Christ’s instruction to enter into the closet, shut the door, and pray to the Father in secret, who sees in secret and rewards openly. Private worship embraces all the elements of devotion exercised by the individual alone with God: secret prayer, in which the soul pours out its confessions, petitions, intercessions, and thanksgivings; the private reading and meditation of the Word, in which God speaks to the soul and the soul ponders His truth; private praise and the singing of psalms; self-examination, in which the heart is searched before God; and the cultivation of communion with God, the soul’s intimate fellowship with its Lord. Private worship holds a peculiar importance as the truest barometer of the spiritual life, for it is exercised with no witness but God, and a man is in religion what he is in secret and no more. Public and family worship may be sustained by habit, duty, or the eyes of others; private worship, hidden from all human view, reveals the real state of the soul. It is the hidden root from which the visible branches of family and public devotion draw their life: a soul vigorous in private worship will flourish in the assembly, while a soul that has deserted its closet will wither, however diligent its outward religion. The believer is therefore to maintain a faithful, regular life of private worship—a set time and place to meet God alone, day by day—giving himself to secret prayer, the Word, meditation, and communion with his Lord. Its neglect is the slow starvation of the soul; its faithful practice is the secret of all vital and growing godliness, the place where the deepest dealings between God and the soul are transacted, and the hidden spring of a fruitful Christian life.

corruption_summary: No major postmodern redefinition, but private worship is widely neglected—the closet deserted, personal devotion abandoned amid distraction and busyness—hollowing out the spiritual life from its hidden root.
corruption_paragraphs: Private worship is corrupted chiefly by neglect—the desertion of the closet that quietly hollows out the whole spiritual life from its hidden root. In an age of ceaseless distraction, perpetual busyness, and the unending demands of screens and devices, the believer’s private devotion is among the first casualties: the set time of secret prayer and the Word is crowded out, deferred, and finally abandoned, until the soul lives without any regular, personal meeting with God alone. A man may maintain his public worship and even his family devotions while his private worship has long since collapsed—and such a soul, whatever its outward appearance, is withering, for private worship is the hidden spring from which the visible branches draw their life. Its neglect is the slow starvation of the soul, often unnoticed until the inward decay shows itself in the outward life.

The recovery of private worship is the recovery of vital, growing godliness at its source. Because it is exercised with no witness but God, private worship is the truest measure of the spiritual life: a man is in religion what he is in his closet and no more. The believer is to maintain a faithful, regular life of private worship—a set time and place to meet God alone, day by day—giving himself to secret prayer, the reading and meditation of the Word, private praise, self-examination, and communion with his Lord. This hidden discipline, faithfully kept, is the secret of all flourishing religion: it feeds the soul, deepens communion with God, fortifies against temptation, and supplies the inward vigor that makes family and public worship come alive. Tend the closet, and the whole life flourishes; desert it, and no outward devotion can long disguise the inward decay. The believer who would grow in grace and walk closely with God must, above all, be faithful in the hidden worship of his secret place, where the deepest dealings between God and the soul are transacted.

etymology: So called because the Lord Jesus taught it; from His instruction, “After this manner therefore pray ye” (Matt 6:9) and “When ye pray, say” (Luke 11:2).
biblical_def: The Lord’s Prayer is the prayer the Lord Jesus taught His disciples—recorded in Matthew 6 and Luke 11—given both as a prayer to be used and as a pattern and rule directing the matter and manner of all true prayer. Christ gave it in response to the disciples’ request, ‘Lord, teach us to pray,’ introducing it with ‘After this manner therefore pray ye’ (a pattern) and ‘When ye pray, say’ (a form to be used). It consists of a preface and six petitions. The preface, ‘Our Father which art in heaven,’ teaches us to approach God with the confidence and reverence of children to a Father, and with others (‘our’), as members of His family. The first three petitions concern God and His glory: ‘Hallowed be thy name’ (that God be honored and reverenced); ‘Thy kingdom come’ (that His reign advance and be consummated); ‘Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven’ (that His will be obeyed and submitted to). The last three concern our needs: ‘Give us this day our daily bread’ (for our temporal provision); ‘Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors’ (for pardon, joined to a forgiving spirit); ‘Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil’ (for grace against sin and the evil one). The doxology, ‘For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen,’ ascribes all to God. The Lord’s Prayer is thus a perfect model of prayer, teaching its right order (God’s glory before our needs), its proper matter (what we ought to ask), its spirit (reverent, dependent, forgiving, submissive), and its scope (God’s name, kingdom, and will; our provision, pardon, and protection). It may be used as a form of words, and has been from the earliest church; but it is chiefly given as a pattern, a rule and directory for all our praying, by which we learn to pray rightly. The catechisms expound it petition by petition as the model of prayer, even as they expound the Decalogue as the model of duty and the Creed as the model of faith.

corruption_summary: The Lord’s Prayer is corrupted by the vain repetition that recites it mechanically and mindlessly—the very fault Christ warned against just before giving it—and by the neglect that ignores it as the pattern for all prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord’s Prayer is corrupted, ironically, into the very fault Christ warned against in the breath before He gave it: ‘use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.’ Given as the cure for vain repetition, the prayer is too often turned into vain repetition itself—recited mechanically, rapidly, and mindlessly, the words rolling off the tongue while the heart is wholly disengaged, treated almost as a magic formula whose mere utterance avails. This empties the prayer of all its meaning and turns the Lord’s gift into the heathen’s babbling. The remedy is not to abandon its use but to pray it thoughtfully, with the understanding and the heart engaged in each petition, as a real address to the Father.

The Lord’s Prayer is corrupted, on the other side, by neglect of its role as the pattern and rule for all prayer. Many who would never recite it mechanically nonetheless ignore the model it provides, praying without the order, matter, and spirit it teaches—rushing to their own needs without first seeking God’s glory, asking amiss because they have not learned from Christ what to ask, praying selfishly, anxiously, or unforgivingly. But the Lord gave the prayer chiefly as a pattern—‘after this manner pray ye’—a directory by which all our praying is to be shaped: God’s name, kingdom, and will sought before our own needs; our provision, pardon, and protection asked in dependence; the whole offered to a Father, with others, in a reverent, submissive, and forgiving spirit. The recovery of the doctrine restores the Lord’s Prayer to both its uses: a form to be prayed thoughtfully and reverently, and—above all—a perfect pattern teaching us how to pray, by which the disciple, like the first disciples, learns from the Lord Himself the matter, order, and spirit of acceptable prayer.
